results.root_cause_actual: PR #4471 raised WORKER_CONCURRENCY from 8 to 32 while DB_POOL_SIZE remained at 10 with max_overflow=0. The pool hard-caps at exactly 10 connections regardless of worker count. With 32 workers all needing DB access and only 10 connections available, 22+ workers are always queued waiting for a connection. The pool_timeout of 30s equals the request timeout of 30s, so any queued worker exhausts its full wait budget and the request fails with HTTP 500. Pool waiters grew continuously from 6 → 19 → 27 → 31 → 44 → 52, until all 32 workers were blocked simultaneously, causing complete service unavailability.
results.root_cause_expected: Deploy v2.14.0 raised WORKER_CONCURRENCY from 8 to 32 while leaving DB_POOL_SIZE at 10 with max_overflow 0, so 32 concurrent workers contend for 10 database connections and block in pool acquire until the 30s timeout, exhausting the connection pool.

judge.reason: Both identify the same underlying cause: a deploy that increased WORKER_CONCURRENCY from 8 to 32 without proportionally increasing DB_POOL_SIZE (kept at 10 with max_overflow 0), causing workers to exhaust the fixed pool and timeout waiting for connections.

results.root_cause_actual: PR #2208 (v3.7.1) introduced an unbounded in-process response cache (_RESPONSE_CACHE: dict[str, list[dict]] = {}) keyed by request_id with no eviction, TTL, or size limit. At ~47.8 RPS with unique request_ids, cache entries accumulated permanently in the module-level dict (512,044 entries, 3.41 GiB by OOMKill), driving RSS monotonically from 412 MB at boot to 4094 MB — the full 4096Mi container memory limit (unchanged from v3.6.9). With no eviction possible and GC unable to reclaim strongly-referenced entries, cgroup reclaim failed and the OOM killer terminated the container (exit 137). Each restart cleared the in-process cache but reloaded the same code, causing repeated OOMKills and CrashLoopBackOff.
results.root_cause_expected: The response cache added in v3.7.1 is an unbounded module-level dict keyed by request_id, so every request inserts a new entry that is never evicted or expired; resident memory grows monotonically until the container is OOMKilled and restarts.

judge.reason: Both identify the same underlying cause: an unbounded module-level response cache dictionary in v3.7.1 with no eviction mechanism that accumulates entries indefinitely, causing monotonic memory growth and OOMKill, with the candidate providing additional implementation details and operational context that are consistent with and support the reference cause.

mechanism: Commit b91f0c74 in PR #2208 deployed at 2026-08-21T07:58Z added a module-level dict _RESPONSE_CACHE: dict[str, list[dict]] = {} with no eviction or expiry mechanism.
Every incoming request with a unique request_id writes its full payload to _RESPONSE_CACHE and nothing is ever removed.
At ~47.8 RPS with unique request_ids, cache entries accumulate continuously: 142,118 entries (~11 min), 352,117 entries (~25 min), 512,044 entries at first OOMKill.
The cache dict alone held 3.41 GiB of memory (confirmed by heap dump at OOMKill), driving RSS from 412 MB at boot to 3,620 MB within ~38 minutes.
GC collected 0 objects because all cache entries are strongly referenced by the module-level dict, preventing any reclamation.
RSS hit the 4096Mi container memory limit, cgroup reclaim failed, and the OOM killer terminated the container (exit 137).
Each restart cleared the in-process cache (RSS reset to ~412 MB), but the same code reloaded and the unbounded accumulation restarted immediately, causing repeated OOMKills and CrashLoopBackOff.

results.root_cause_actual: PR #881 (api-gateway v9.2.0, deployed 18:40:00Z) raised the gateway's PAYMENTS_READ_TIMEOUT from 3s to 30s and disabled the circuit breaker. The critical value mismatch is: gateway read timeout (30s) > ALB proxy_read_timeout (10s, unchanged since 2024). When the partner acquirer latency spiked to 12.4s at 18:47Z, the ALB reached its 10s limit and returned 504 to clients, but the gateway thread did not abort — it continued holding the upstream connection for up to 29.9s of the 30s timeout. With the circuit breaker removed, every new payment request also consumed a thread for the full 30s rather than failing fast. Threads accumulated faster than they were freed; all 64 gateway worker threads became blocked in PaymentsClient.execute() by 18:51Z. With no free threads, the RejectedExecutionException was thrown for every inbound request regardless of route, causing /v1/orders and /v1/catalog — endpoints that do not touch payments-svc — to also return 504, dropping gateway availability to 88.1%.
results.root_cause_expected: PR #881 raised the gateway's payments-svc read timeout from 3s to 30s (and disabled the circuit breaker) while the edge load balancer's proxy_read_timeout stayed at 10s. When partner latency rose, the edge cut clients off at 10s with 504s while gateway worker threads stayed pinned on the upstream call for the full 30s, saturating the 64-thread pool and taking down routes that never touch payments-svc.

judge.reason: Both identify the same underlying cause: PR #881's mismatch between the raised 30s gateway timeout and the unchanged 10s ALB timeout, combined with the disabled circuit breaker, which allowed threads to block for extended periods and exhaust the thread pool.

results.root_cause_actual: Migration 0042_backfill_order_status (PR #1157) dropped idx_orders_customer_id, which was the index serving every hot-path customer order-history query (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50) at ~312 requests/second. Without this index, PostgreSQL fell back to full sequential scans across all 41.2M rows of the orders table. With ~309 such scans per second, blocks read per second rose 240x (1,240 → 298,000), saturating db-prod-2 CPU from 24% to 99%, driving mean query time to 5,910ms and p99 HTTP latency from 210ms to 9,800ms — a 14x SLO burn rate breach. The 10,000ms statement timeout only partially mitigated the damage, cancelling the slowest queries while still allowing multi-second degraded responses.

mechanism: Migration 0042_backfill_order_status executed at 2026-08-25T02:00:00Z and issued DROP INDEX idx_orders_customer_id at 02:00:04Z.
The hot-path query 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50' had previously been served by idx_orders_customer_id on every customer order-history request.
With idx_orders_customer_id gone and no replacement index on customer_id, the query planner chose a full sequential scan across all 41.2M rows.
Sequential scans per minute on orders exploded from 2 to 18,402; index scans collapsed from 18,660 to 41 per minute.
Each sequential scan reads the entire 41.2M row table, driving postgres_blocks_read_per_sec from 1,240 to 298,000 (240x increase).
The massive I/O demand saturated db-prod-2 CPU (24% → 99%) and caused query latency to reach 5,910ms mean and 6.2s+ for individual calls.
p99 HTTP request duration spiked from 210ms to 9,800ms, breaching the 0.5s SLO at 14x burn rate and triggering statement timeouts and HTTP 500s.

results.root_cause_actual: PR #3302 (commit e5710b93) in notify-service v4.1.0 rewrote the retry policy in notify/delivery.py with three compounding misconfigurations in relation to the sms-provider's documented 500 req/s hard limit: (1) backoff_factor changed from 0.5 to 0.0, making all retry sleeps evaluate to 0.0s; (2) respect_retry_after changed from True to False, causing the sms-provider's Retry-After: 30s header to be ignored; (3) max_attempts raised from 3 to 10 and retry_on_status expanded to include 429, 400, 401, and 404. With inbound load of ~500 msg/s and max_attempts=10, the theoretical maximum outbound rate was 5000 req/s — 10x the 500 req/s contract limit. Once the sms-provider returned its first 429 at 11:22:45Z, each rate-limited response triggered 9 additional zero-delay retries (each also receiving 429s), creating a self-amplifying request storm that drove outbound traffic to 5140 req/s (10.3x the contract limit) within 20 seconds, caused 96% of responses to be 429s, and led to account suspension at 11:33:02Z with SMS delivery dropping to zero.
results.root_cause_expected: PR #3302 rewrote the outbound retry policy to 10 attempts with backoff_factor 0.0, stopped respecting Retry-After, and added 4xx statuses (429/400/401/404) to the retry list. Every 429 from sms-provider is retried immediately up to 10 times, amplifying a 500 req/s workload into 5140 req/s — a self-sustaining retry storm that pushed the provider to 96% 429s and then suspended the account.

judge.reason: Both identify the same underlying cause: PR #3302's retry policy rewrite that changed backoff_factor to 0.0, disabled Retry-After respect, increased max_attempts to 10, and added 4xx statuses to retry_on_status, creating a self-sustaining retry storm that amplified load from ~500 req/s to 5140 req/s and triggered account suspension.

mechanism: PR #3302 deployed notify-service v4.1.0 at 11:15:00Z, changing backoff_factor from 0.5 to 0.0, respect_retry_after from True to False, max_attempts from 3 to 10, and adding 429/400/401/404 to retry_on_status.
At 11:22:45Z the sms-provider returned a 429 with Retry-After: 30s, indicating the 500 req/s rate limit was breached.
Because respect_retry_after=False, the Retry-After header was ignored; because backoff_factor=0.0, all retry sleeps evaluated to 0.0s; retries fired immediately.
Because 429 was now in retry_on_status and max_attempts=10, each rate-limited response triggered 9 additional immediate retries, each of which also received 429s and triggered further retries.
Outbound request rate spiked from 512/s to 5140/s within 20 seconds, reaching 10.3x the 500 req/s contract limit.
96% of sms-provider responses became 429; mean retry attempts per message hit 9.94 (max of 10), and retries on 4xx reached 41,200/min.
Egress bandwidth rose from 61 Mbps to 940 Mbps (15x baseline), confirming the retry storm was consuming network resources.
The sms-provider suspended the notify-service account at 11:33:02Z for sustained abuse of the rate limit at 10x contract rate, dropping SMS delivery to zero.

results.root_cause_actual: PR #5540 (commit 0c88fe41) made three changes that combined to cause a recurring cache stampede: (1) CACHE_FLUSH_ON_DEPLOY set to true caused all ~12,900 cache keys to be written within the same second at deploy (06:00:00Z); (2) CACHE_TTL_JITTER_SECONDS reduced from 60 to 0 meant every key received an identical 300s TTL with no spread, so all ~12,900 keys expire in the same 1-second bucket every 300 seconds (first at 06:05:00Z, repeating at 06:10, 06:15, 06:20, 06:25); (3) CACHE_SINGLEFLIGHT removed from true to false meant every concurrent cache-miss request issued its own independent SELECT to Postgres instead of coalescing. The collision between the synchronized expiry (12,910 keys/bucket) and Postgres's unchanged max_connections=200 (normally consumed by only 44 connections) caused psycopg.OperationalError: too many clients already, cache refill failure, and 503s — repeating every 5 minutes for the duration of the incident.
results.root_cause_expected: PR #5540 set CACHE_TTL_JITTER_SECONDS to 0 and removed the single-flight guard, while the deploy flushed the whole cache at once. All ~12.9k keys were written in the same second and now expire in the same second, so every 300s the entire cache misses simultaneously and thousands of identical queries stampede Postgres, exhausting max_connections and returning 503s in a 6-second burst every 5 minutes.

judge.reason: Both identify the same three specific changes in PR #5540 (CACHE_TTL_JITTER_SECONDS set to 0, removal of single-flight guard, and cache flush on deploy) and the same mechanism by which they combined to cause synchronized cache expiry and connection exhaustion, with only minor differences in phrasing and level of detail.

mechanism: PR #5540 set CACHE_FLUSH_ON_DEPLOY=true, flushing all Redis keys at 06:00:00Z and forcing a cold-cache warm-up where all ~12,900 keys were written within the same second.
PR #5540 set CACHE_TTL_JITTER_SECONDS from 60 to 0, so every key received an identical TTL of exactly 300s with no spread.
With zero jitter, all ~12,900 keys expire in the same 1-second bucket, exactly 300s (5 minutes) after they were written — first at 06:05:00Z, then 06:10:00Z, 06:15:00Z, 06:20:00Z, 06:25:00Z.

PR #5540 also removed the single-flight lock (singleflight.lock per product_id), so every request that arrives during the expiry window issues its own independent SELECT to Postgres instead of coalescing behind one writer.
The combined flood of ~2,900–3,400 concurrent identical SELECTs drives db_qps from a baseline of ~180 to over 3,300 in under 1 second.
The surge exhausts the Postgres max_connections limit of 200 (normally used by only 44 connections), causing psycopg.OperationalError: too many clients already.
With Postgres refusing connections, cache-refill queries fail, the cache cannot be repopulated, and HTTP requests return 503s — a pattern repeating every 5 minutes for the duration of the incident.

ruled_out.candidate: Traffic increase causing DB overload
ruled_out.why_not: Traffic was explicitly flat at 1840 rps all morning, identical to the previous Thursday (confirmed in both application.log and deployment.txt), so no external demand increase can explain the periodic spikes.

ruled_out.candidate: Postgres configuration change (max_connections reduction or migration)
ruled_out.why_not: deployment.txt states 'Postgres db-prod-3 unchanged, max_connections=200, no migration today.' The connection limit was not changed; it was simply overwhelmed by the stampede.

ruled_out.candidate: CACHE_FLUSH_ON_DEPLOY alone as root cause
ruled_out.why_not: Flushing the cache on deploy causes an initial cold-cache warm-up spike (observed at 06:00–06:01), which recovered within ~90 seconds. The recurring every-5-minute pattern is explained only by jitter removal causing synchronized expiry; without jitter removal, the flush alone would not produce the repeating sawtooth pattern.

ruled_out.candidate: Removal of single-flight guard alone as root cause
ruled_out.why_not: Removing single-flight amplifies the blast radius of each stampede but does not by itself cause keys to expire simultaneously. Without synchronized expiry (caused by zero jitter), the stampedes would be spread across keys expiring at different times and would not overwhelm Postgres.
